I forbindelse med ophævelse af opkrævningslovens § 17, stk. 1, nr. 3, ved lov nr. 1441 af 22. december 2004 ændredes grundlaget for fastsættelse af sanktioner for overtrædelse af kildeskatteloven. Der er nu en dom fra Østre Landsret, der fastslår, at sanktionen for en overtrædelse af kildeskatteloven, hvor den forsætlige unddragelse er over 100.000 kr., svarer til en overtrædelse af skattekontrolloven.. Fastsættelse af kildeskattebøder 1. Indledning I forbindelse med ophævelsen af opkrævningslovens § 17, stk. 1, nr. 3, ved lov nr. 1441 af 22. december 2004 ændredes grundlaget for fastsættelsen af strafansvaret ved overtrædelse af kildeskatteloven. Problemet blev drøftet med Rigsadvokaten i 2005, og det blev besluttet, at der skulle anlægges prøvesager til fastsættelse af en takstmæssig bøde for overtrædelse af de sanktionerede bestemmelser i kildeskattelovgivningen. 2. Praksis I to domme fra 2006 har overtrædelse af kildeskattelovens § 74, stk. 2, jf. stk. 1, nr. 1, 2 og 3, været til pådømmelse. Det drejer sig om Østre Landsretsdommen af 25. august 2006 refereret i SKM2006.520.ØLR og dom af 21. september 2006 fra Københavns Byret. I begge sager blev der fastsat en tillægsbøde svarende til en gang de unddragne A-skatter. Der er således retspraksis for, at overtrædelse af kildeskatteloven, hvor man undlader at foretage indeholdelse af A-skat mv., jf. kildeskattelovens § 74, stk. 2, jf. stk. 1, nr. 1 afgiver urigtige eller vildledende oplysninger til brug for angivelse af A-skat m.v., jf. kildeskattelovens § 74, stk. 2, jf. stk. 1, nr. 2 og 3, straffes på samme måde, som ved overtrædelse af skattekontrolloven og momsloven, når der er tale om forsæt til unddragelse. 2.1. Sager hvor unddragelsen overstiger 100.000 kr. Det følger heraf, at i kildeskattesager, hvor den forsætlige unddragelse overstiger 100.000 kr., skal der nedlægges påstand om en frihedsstraf og en tillægsbøde svarende til en gang den unddragne A-skat. Dette gælder også overtrædelse af kildeskattelovens § 75, nr. 1, hvor man lader sig udbetale løn uden, at der er indeholdt A-skat. Der kan også være tale om fortielse af oplysninger eller uregistreret virksomhed. Hvis forholdet er omfattet af opkrævningslovens § 17, rejses der tiltale efter denne bestemmelse i stedet for kildeskatteloven. 3. Prøvesager Rigsadvokaten har bestemt, der skal anlægges prøvesager, som kan danne grundlag for den administrative praksis. Det er ud fra ovennævnte domme nærliggende at antage, at domstolene vil godkende en bødepraksis i kildeskattesagerne, svarende til bøderne ved overtrædelse af skattekontrolloven og momsloven, når der er tale om unddragelse. Fastsættelsen af sanktion skal ske i de sager, hvor unddragelsen er sket den 1. januar 2005 og senere. Der skal derfor nedlægges påstand om straf efter det takstmæssige bødesystem og svarende til bødestørrelsen for unddragen skat og moms. Bøden beregnes således: I kildeskattesager, hvor unddragelsen ikke overstiger 100.000 kr. og med forsæt til unddragelse ved overtrædelse af kildeskatteloven, fastsættes bøden til 2 gange den samlede unddragelse. Ved grov uagtsomhed udgør bøden 1 gang den samlede unddragelse. Af den del af unddragelsen, der ikke overstiger 30.000 kr., beregnes bøden dog kun som 1 gang den unddragne A-skat ved forsæt, og som halvdelen af den unddragne A-skat ved grov uagtsomhed. Hvis der foreligger både et forsætligt forhold og et groft uagtsomt forhold ved unddragelse af kildeskatteloven, foretages nedsættelsen af normalbøden til halvdelen af de første 30.000 kr. af den unddragne A-skat, såvel for det beløb, der vedrører det forsætlige forhold, som for det beløb, der vedrører det groft uagtsomme forhold. Såfremt der er tale om andre overtrædelser af skatte- og momslovgivningen, skal den samlede unddragelse lægges til grund for bødeberegningen. Der er således tale om et takstmæssigt bødesystem med fuld kumulation. 4. Ikrafttræden og virkning Disse retningslinier træder i kraft med øjeblikkelig virkning, idet administrative afgørelser fortsat er sat i bero, indtil der foreligger afgørelser i prøvesagerne. Evangelisten Mathæus fortæller kortfattet, hvordan en rig mand Josef fra Arimetæa beder Pilatus om tilladelse til at begrave den døde. Josef får lov, og sammen med andre svøber han den døde ind i et liglagen og lægger det i en grav, som straks lukkes til med en stor sten.
Hvad nu sker mellem Jesu gravlæggelse og opstandelse påskemorgen lægger hen i mørket. Hvad dog ikke hindrer eftertidens dramatiske skildringer af hvad fandt sted i dette intermezzo: nemlig Jesu nedstigning i dødsriget og hans opvækkelse og oprejsning af de døde.

I salmerne til påskelørdag møder vi en kosmisk kampplads mellem det gode og det onde, mellem liv og død, Gud og Djævel.

I år påskelørdag vil jeg gerne trække en af bipersonerne frem, nemlig Josef af Arimethea.
Han skygger ikke for hovedpersonen, Jesus, men han træder frem som en, som vi kan se til i vores liv.
Josef fra Arimethea går frem foran Pilatus og beder om lov til at begrave den døde.
Han har ikke lagt sit lod i mængdens råb og had, men han finder derimod sin visdom i Kristus.
I den kristne tradition helt siden tidlig tid er Josef af Arimethea derfor også blev sammenl⟦ignet⟧ med og set som det retfærdige og lykkelige menneske, som er nævnt hos den gammeltestamentlige salmedigter i den allerførste salme i Salmernes Bog.
Salme 1 i Det gamle Testamente lyder:
Salmedigteren kunne måske her tænke på sig selv som den lykkelige eller læst med kristne briller tænke på Kristus som den retfærdige og den lykkelige, men op igennem tiden finder vi flere udlægninger, hvor netop Josef fra Arimethea bliver set som en personificering af den lykkelige, af den, som gør det rette.
Den tolkning kendes både fra kommentarer og illustrationer. Og jeg faldt for nylig over en illustration fra den ortodokse serbiske kirke, som viser Josef af Arimethea i forbindelse med salme 1 i det gamle Testamente, altså i forbindelse med netop denne gammeltestamentlige salme.
Hvad er det med Josef fra Arimethea. Jo, Josef gør det rigtige i situationen. Han har nok gået stille med dørene indtil nu, men ved Jesu død træder han i karakter, insister på en ordentlig begravelse af den døde, som for dermed at signalere sin dybe respekt for og tillid til Jesus.
Josef af Arimethea, siger de oldkirkelige fædre, følger således ikke blot i hælene på de ugudeliges råd, som var at henrette Jesus og gøre ham til intet. Josef så mere i Jesus end en oprører, en blasfemiker og forbryder. Og det er jo netop også, hvad evangeliet forkynder.
Kirkefaderen Hieronimus, som levede i begyndelsen af det femte århundrede, skriver, at vi skal se den retfærdige mand, som er omtalt i salme 1, som Josef af Arimethea. For han spejler, hvad gør en retfærdig mand og kvinde, nemlig et menneske, som ikke lader sig nøje med visdommen i alt, hvad vi mennesker selv finder på, men han finder den dybeste visdom og sandhed, ja livet i den korsfæstede Jesus Kristus.

When Joel's life was abruptly ended by a nunchaku at the local bowling alley, it is up to Detective Winston to interrogate the prime suspects: Rosemary and Mia, in this chilling game of strike or spare.

Kneading the stub of his cigarette into the worn-out ashtray, Winston's gaze flitted between the photographs in front of him. A bowling alley, deserted, save for a solitary figure slumped over in the congealing slick of his own blood – the scene drenched in a chilling morbidity. 

His suspect was Mia, a waitress at the bowling alley. The late shift was her domain; her eyes, always heavy-lidded with fatigue, had fallen on a familiar figure, Joel, numbingly often. The man had his peculiar habits, including late-night bowling. Mia had a keen knowledge of that; it wasn’t easy to overlook when they regularly crossed paths during her shifts, Joel’s ball thundering and skidding down the shiny lanes.

Fiddling with a small, old key on his desk, Winston’s thought went back to his first meeting with Mia. He had found the key while cleaning her table after an interview and asked her about it. Almost flippantly, she mentioned it was for a private mausoleum in the nearby cemetery. The location was within walking distance from her workplace, an old cemetery cloaked in a gloom that seemed centuries old. The eerie part was her odd ritual; post her shift, her coworkers attested to seeing her trudge towards the graveyard regularly, a private pilgrimage in the dead of night.

Winston vividly remembered his surprise when he had found nunchaku, a pair of them, while searching Mia's home. The night visits to the cemetery coupled with the ominous presence of the martial arts weapon was undoubtedly unsettling. Unraveling further, he found out Mia had been practicing and honing her skills with the nunchaku at home, late into the night. For years, she had been devoted to martial arts, with a particular emphasis on the nunchaku, the significance of which crept up on him like a poisonous vine. Her gym was known for teaching the use of this weapon.

"I suspect you're quite adept at swinging these," Winston had said to Mia, gesturing towards the nunchaku that lay on the table between them when he'd confronted her about it later. 

Mia had smiled enigmatically, her eyes twinkling with the lethality of secrets untold. "Keep your eyes open, detective," she had replied, her voice a chilling sotto voce lingering between them, hang enough in the suffocating silence.

His thoughts whirling, Winston stubbed out the last of his cigarette. The available evidence was yet⟦ to⟧ form a coherent story, but Mia was conspicuous. He had ventured into labyrinthian investigations before, but the mystery of Joel's murder felt like uncharted territory. Winston felt a shiver creep into his spine as he got ready for round two with Mia.

Winston stepped into the dimly lit bowling alley, prowling between lanes like a panther on the hunt. Winston, drizzly and cold from the rain, squinted at the farmhouse across the gloomy countryside. The hunting shop sign creaking in the wind was a well-known fixture having Gordon's name inscribed in bold on the top. Winston knew very well that the shop was run by Gordon, who was as good a supplier of hunting equipment as he was a farmer. The murder of Harry, now known in newspapers as "The Chalet Bear Trap Murder," had to be untangled.

In front of Winston, a rough-faced man, smeared with sweat and dust from his work at both the shop and the farm, set to work, carrying feed bags to the barn. It was Gordon, the local farmer in question.

"Hello, Gordon," - Winston greeted him.

"Howdy, got no time to chat. Gotta feed the animals before the weather worsens. These parts, we got some bear problems," - Gordon grunted in response.

Catching a break, Winston moved towards the subject. "I heard you had some form of disagreement with Harry at the farmer's market a while back."

Scoffing, Gordon refused to meet his gaze. "Sure, we had words... I wasn't selling much, and he was selling everything. Fella won an award recently for his agricultural products while the market for my products was going under."

"You blame Harry for that?" - Winston asked, laying the facts bare.

"Goddam right I do..." - Gordon muttered, throwing a dirty sack onto a pile.

"Where were you at the time Harry was killed, Gordon?"

The farmer dusted his hands, meeting Winston's gaze with defiance. "I was here, at the farm. All day. You can ask anyone around."

“As for the chalet where poor Harry met his end..." - Winston started.

“Yeah, Harry was at my chalet. It’s my property, and I’m the who decides who can or can't access it." - Gordon interrupted, more flustered now.

"Did you see anyone else around that day?"

"Nope. Quiet as a mouse that day, just the bears and me."

After that, silence fell over the now dark homestead. Winston considered the facts, the countryside, farm, bears, the market, the struggling sales, it all called for further investigation. But for now, he just tipped his hat and walked back to his car under the drizzling rain, leaving a brooding Gordon to his work.

As the sheer size of the chalet murder scene could overwhelm a lesser detective, Winston, stood firm. The victim, Harry, was a known critic within the food industry. His sharp tongue had a penchant for landing him in a hot stew of trouble. This time, it would seem, there was a rogue ingredient he just couldn't swallow.

Winston strolled over to Dexter, a known acquaintance of Harry's and an avid food enthusiast himself. The man's love for fine cuisine was matched only by his fervour for his religion.

"Evening, Dexter," Winston began. "How are you holding up?"

"I'm doing okay... under the circumstances." Dexter wasn't the most expressive despite his harsh critiques.

"I heard Harry was very open about his thoughts on your religious beliefs," Winston continued.

Dexter sighed, "Yes, he publicly mocked my⟦ faith⟧ during an event. Disrespectful, but that was just Harry."

"Dexter," Winston turned back to him, "I noticed a photograph of you and Tony the Tooth having dinner together surfaced on social media. Where were you the night of Harry's death?"

Dexter's association with him, especially in a photograph in a restaurant notoriously frequented by other criminals, only bred more suspicion.

Changing tactics, Winston delved into Dexter's rural interests. Dexter's love for hunting was no secret to the community; he was often seen in the woods around the outskirts of the town. One of the common pieces of equipment in his collection was bear traps, which he frequently used in the woods. Dexter was often seen studying these traps, enhancing his understanding of them.

"Care to show me your hunting gear?" Winston suddenly asked, catching him off guard.

"Sure, I guess," Dexter replied tensely. He led the way to a shed, where hunting equipment including rifles and the commonly used bear traps littered the floor and walls.

Inside the buzzing hubbub of the city's most popular recording studio, Ivan's death by snake venom sends shockwaves through the music realm, forcing the indomitable Detective Winston to pierce the veil of sound and silence, suspects, Timothy and Ricky, echoing in his ears.

The flashing lights and the police tape painted a macabre picture outside the recording studio where Ivan was pronounced dead. Detective Winston stared at the dispatch report and heaved a weary sigh. Highlighted information spelled out a sad tale of love, jealousy, and secrets; especially the ones contained in Timothy's silent confession of an argument where Ivan confronted him about the affair with his girlfriend.

As he entered the studio, a peculiar detail stood out – it was empty when the victim was found. The police had taken the usual preliminary measures, clearing the premises as they went. That detail played a repetitive note in Winston's mind. There was only one name that matched the time of death, Timothy.

Begrudgingly, he agreed to interview Timothy, the victim’s friend and⟦ also⟧ a surfing instructor by trade. Timothy's van was a shrine to waxed boards of all sizes, shapes, and colors, almost like weapons of battle against the waves. When Winston had asked him about it, Timothy fondly explained that every board had its unique purpose, for each wave and beach condition. His job demanded him to know places, waves, and beaches in intimate detail. One could even notice the envy tinged bitterness in Timothy's voice when he shared his love for discovering new surfing spots and how Ivan’s musical success overshadowed his own aspirations.

“What brings you here, detective?” Timothy's voice cut through Winston's thoughts. “Well, you were last seen here with Ivan. You guys…"

“Yeah, we were working on a music project together,” Timothy finished Winston's half-spoken question. His face turned a shade darker as he added, “That was our thing, you know. He did the music, I brought the vibe. But everyone always loved Ivan more, even my own girlfriend.”

There was a certain restlessness in Timothy's manner. His eyes kept darting towards the door, his van in sight. It was always packed and ready; 'to chase the waves,' Timothy had shared during the friendly chit-chat. His resentment towards Ivan had resurfaced, amplified by the fact that Ivan's girlfriend was now in love with him.

When Winston mentioned Ivan's girlfriend, Timothy's smile tightened. Yet when he asked about the argument where Ivan had confronted him about the affair, the smile faded away completely. He didn't want to expose sharper edges of their relationship; the complex, fraught friendship woven with threads of rivalry and jealousy. Most of all, there was a looming fear of Ivan revealing their secret affair to the world.

Winston slowly stood up, giving Timothy a knowing look. He thanked him for his time and walked away, leaving an unsettling silence behind him as Timothy sat, staring at the spot where Ivan used to create music. His secret was a festering wound he had no idea how to treat, and the fear of exposure was a haunting melody he couldn't escape.

At the end of a long day, Winston found himself standing on the bridge, gazing at the dark and unyielding ocean. The carefully collected facts played on repeat, like a song stuck in a loop. He couldn't help but think of Timothy, his passions, his secrets, his fear, his jealousy, and his time at the studio which eerily aligned with the irrevocable end of Ivan's life. A hazy picture began to take form in his mind, but he knew it was far from complete...There were still missing notes in this haunting symphony of death.

Detective Winston stepped out of his car and straightened his tie as he made his way towards the pet shop. An older man stood at the entrance, a look of potential fear and regret on his face.

"Detective Winston," he introduced himself and showed his badge. He noticed a change in Ricky's demeanor. "Might we have a word regarding your business?"

Ricky, swallowing hard, nodded and gestured to the back room of the pet shop. It was filled with a variety of animals, among them a large, intimidating venomous snake settled in a glass tank, aptly showcased as the shop's specialty.

"You seem to have quite a variety of pets here, and appropriate paperwork on display. You do legally own this place, don't you?" Winston asked, pointing at the legal documents hanging on the wall.

Ricky, still unsettled, nodded, "Yes. I also know a bit about venom extraction, which makes this business unique," he added with an attempt at lightheartedness. 

"You know, the police got a tip-off about some illegal activity regarding this pet shop," Winston continued. Ricky's eyes widened.

"Why, I've no idea what you're insinuating detective," Ricky stuttered, looking like a man who feared impending financial and legal repercussions.

"Your financial situation hasn't been the best we've heard," Winston said, "and someone named Ivan has been feeding us some rather interesting information regarding your debts."

"Ivan." Ricky whispered under his breath.

"It seems you had a private meeting with Ivan in an empty recording studio," Winston revealed, seeing Ricky's surprise at this information. "That's where he recorded your conversation, and you confessed to some illegal activities, didn't you?"

Ricky looked down and then glanced up, resignation in his eyes. He nodded somberly, "Yes, Ivan was the only one who knew about the illegal activities... He recorded me talking about the illegal sales and has been blackmailing me with the recording."

Winston thanked Ricky for his time and walked out of the pet shop with much to ponder about this case. One thing was certain - the recording studio where Ricky made his confession was going to be his next stop.<turn|>

Winston stared at the case file on his desk, a half-drunk cup of cold coffee to his side. The victim, Troy, had been found dead in a shopping mall in one of the most unusual circumstances he'd seen: in a bear trap. It was a gruesome scene and one that didn't make much sense.

Confused, Winston made his way to Clyde's auto repair shop. A greasy, dust-covered sign welcoming customers and a few older model cars dotted the yard. The mound of mechanical traps of all kinds added an eerie touch to the scene.

"Clyde," he asked, when a haggard man emerged wiping motor oil off of his hands.

"That's me." came the terse reply.

Winston introduced himself and saw Clyde pause for a moment before shaking his hand. He told him that he wanted to know more about Troy, who according to the information he gathered, was a regular customer at Clyde's.

After a sigh, he nodded, his gaze darkening. "Yeah, Troy was a good customer. Always had car troubles. But he was into me pretty deep... owed me some dough for the work I had done."

Winston then shared a piece of information that Clyde didn't seem privy to - Troy had been at the mall earlier in the day, just before his untimely death.

It was at this point Winston noticed a bear trap amongst the litter of mechanical devices. "You work on those too?" He gestured towards the trap, appearing casual.

Clyde glanced at the trap and nodded. "Sometimes. For pest control and such. People bring them in, they're not workin' right, I fix 'em."

Clyde then went on about how he was on the brink of closing the shop due to his financial struggles. He needed to constantly upgrade his equipment but lacked the necessary funds to do so.

In fact, he too had been at the mall on the same day as Troy. "I was there to buy new equipment for the shop," Clyde added.

It was interesting, Winston thought, given that Clyde's shop was practically a stone's throw away from the location of the murder. He made a mental note to follow-up on that.

As Winston thanked Clyde and turned to leave, he noticed a large sign hanging on the wall with the bold letters stating, "We fix all traps – yes, even bear traps."

Well, he thought to himself, that's a lot of loose ends to tie up. As he walked away, he felt the faint stirrings of a puzzle starting to form. He only hoped he could solve it in time.

In the dim light of an abandoned factory, Kaylee's lifeless body lay with the cold steel of a pickaxe lodged within, thrusting Detective Winston into a dark game of deception with suspects Penelope and Francis.

Winston breathed a sigh of relief as he entered the comfort of his car, escaping the oppressive heat outside. The day had been anything but a usual one and he reviewed the paper on his clipboard yet again. Kaylee, a young woman, was found dead in an abandoned factory of all places and the purported weapon was a pickaxe, an old miner's pickaxe to be exact.

His next interview was scheduled with a nanny named Penelope. Penelope was not your average nanny. Alongside her formal education in early child care, she also had professional training in the same field, acquiring skills that allowed her to excel in handling children. Despite her credible qualifications, Winston found it decidedly strange to connect a nanny with such a gruesome find, not least because Penelope herself had most of her busy day spent with children, not in an old factory.

After a short walk, he approached a modest suburban home quite close to the abandoned factory. The home itself, despite its proximity, seemed worlds apart from the grim discovery location. 

Penelope greeted him at the door, shaking his hand with a warm smile. "Hello, Penelope." Winston greeted, then a thought hit⟦ him⟧. A person of her profession is typically responsible for a child's growth and upbringing. Penelope's studied and trained background in childcare had indeed stuck in his mind since their last encounter.

During their conversation, Winston learned that Penelope was seen leaving her house around the estimated time of the murder. Interestingly enough, he even had a witness claiming to see Penelope with an old mining pickaxe earlier that day, a claim solidly backed up as the recovered pickaxe, the very same weapon used in the murder, matched exactly the one described by the witness.

Just as he was thinking about the pickaxe, a piece of evidence from the crime scene flashed across his mind. Winston reached into his jacket pocket to pull out a page from a diary. It was from Kaylee's diary. The entry was clear; Kaylee had a meeting scheduled with Penelope at the so-called abandoned factory.

A unease washed over Winston, making the usually delicious coffee taste sour in his mouth. Kaylee seemed to have known something about Penelope that she didn't want public. She had unearthed something about Penelope's past... maybe even criminal past. The parents didn't know... and Kaylee was planning to tell.

He glanced at Penelope, who was sitting across from him, looking anxious. She must've known that the exposure would cause her serious embarrassment... and at worst, cost her her job. With no other events reported that could have prevented Kaylee from meeting Penelope, it all looped back to the meeting at the factory.

"Well, Penelope, I do have a long walk back to my car." he said, finishing the last of his coffee and standing up. "I've taken enough of your time, thank you for your cooperation." He gave a nod as he reached the door, leaving the nanny to contemplate her day filled with children, and his with unanswered questions.

Detective Winston grimaced, finally setting down the carefully documented police case file of the late Kaylee. The coffee stains on the file folder began to bleed into the corners of the cover. The pangs of guilt for indulging in too much work in the form of an overbrewed cup of joe were not his only concern. An image haunted him; it was from a video footage where Francis had caught Kaylee red-handed, threatening his daughter which he digitally recorded as proof.

Shaking the sudden chill from his spine, Winston looked out of his office window to the abandoned factory where Kaylee had been found. Francis, Kaylee's husband, had years of mining experience and was renowned for his pickaxe expertise. Francis had arranged the meeting point and was seen coaxing her into trusting that the factory would be undisturbed.

The town had all been abuzz with this unthinkable murder. Kaylee's constant torment of Francis' daughter, enough to induce anxiety and depression in the child, was now common knowledge. Even more upsetting was the unusual delicateness Francis had shown in handling this situation, a man known for his work involving grueling physical labor that required a high level of strength and endurance.

Digging into his pocket Winston pulled out the receipt for the pickaxe that he'd found in Francis’ pocket, a peculiar coincidence considering Francis’ mining background and the tool associated with it.

In the corner of his foul-smelling, second-hand leather bound desk was a photograph. A crisp, clear frame showing Francis purchasing the said pickaxe at the local hardware store. It was not surprising that Francis had chosen to arm himself with a tool he was already so familiar with, but to invite his wife into a murderous trap of his creation was another level of distressing reality.

Winston looked up to see Francis standing in the doorway, tall and solemn. "Detective Winston," he said quietly, "We need to talk about Kaylee."

Winston nodded, gesturing for him to take a seat. "I heard about what happened. About the threats she made to your daughter."

Francis looked taken aback, his gaze shifting around the room. "Yes...I caught her threatening our daughter. I don't know why she couldn't see what her actions were doing to our daughter."

Winston nodded but said nothing. He stayed silent, letting Francis explain in his own time, about the factory meeting he'd arranged with Kaylee, his knowledge that the factory would have been empty at that time, the purchased pickaxe and the chilling threats Kaylee had aimed towards his daughter.

As Francis left his office, Winston glanced back at the file, picking up the coffee cup, he pondered the gritty mysteries life tended to serve up.<turn|>

In the cold echo of a deserted hockey rink, Otis was found dead from a grenade explosion, and now Detective Winston must decipher the clues, suspecting Ervin and Andrew are somehow involved.

Winston let out a pensive sigh as the medical examiner rattled off the factors that spelled foul play, namely the shrapnel directly linked to a grenade. When you see something new, you remember it, he mused.

The town had been buzzing since⟦ Er⟧vin's angry outburst in the synagogue last Sunday. Bystanders had recounted to Winston how Ervin had been shouting at a particular customer he had been consulting with, before the outburst escalated and he stormed off into the synagogue. The same customer Walter Harrison was who Ervin had consulted with before he stormed off into the synagogue, had recounted it to him with fear in his voice.

"And you say you were trembling after the confrontation, Mr. Harrison?" Winston asked after the customer finished recounting Ervin's worrying reaction.

"N-not just a confrontation," the distressed customer stammered, "Ervin, our Rabbi, he lost it – punching the walls, shouting at everyone. There’s still a visible dent where he hit."

Winston gave a slight nod, “Thank you for your cooperation,” he said before heading toward the synagogue to track down Rabbi Ervin.

Ervin Thornberg, the Rabbi, met Winston's inquiring gaze coolly. Ervin had a hardened look - the clear evidence of his military past. He was known in town as former military officer with specialized training in demolitions. Nothing could erase that part of his life.

"Quite an impressive array of memorabilia here, Rabbi," Winston remarked, scanning the room filled with various wartime relics like grenades and medals from Ervin's service days. "Your friends often tell stories of you proudly showing these off."

"Careful with those, Detective, they are from my time in the service," Ervin replied, with a hint of nostalgia creeping into his tone. "My friends, they have a way of making things sound more dramatic."

Winston was further intrigued by the hint of gossip he received from one of Ervin's neighbors, "You know, Otis had been vocal lately. He saw something he shouldn't about Ervin and the synagogue funds. Even said he was planning to go to the authorities."

With that information, Winston pitched it to Ervin, "I hear Otis saw something alarming involving you and the synagogue's funds. Heard he was seriously considering going to the authorities."

Ervin stiffened noticeably, his cool gaze flickered for a moment. "Otis talks too much," he muttered, a subtle hint of annoyance in his tone.

Just as he was about to leave, a troubling fact popped back into his mind - Otis. Otis had seen Ervin embezzling funds from the Synagogue and Ervin knew that. Winston marked it down mentally and with a brisk nod to Rabbi Ervin, made his exit. Feeling the sharp gaze of Ervin boring into his back, he needed no further confirmation.

The pieces were neatly aligning, like pieces of a puzzle, Winston could see it - But it wasn't his place to tell the story, rather gather it. So with another sigh, he slid into the driver's seat and drove off. The knot in his gut tightened as he pulled away from the synagogue - he knew his work here was far from done.

Winston pulled the collar of his jacket up and stepped into the freezing cold of the hockey rink. Alone in the rink, he squinted under the heat of the artificial light to read the deserted stands and make out the chalk lines: "Just a man and his routine...Otis was always here at this time, when no one else was present...So why Otis? Why here?"

Hours later, Winston found himself wading through the mud and foliage of a nearby hiking trail. He was there to meet Andrew, the local hiking guide, a formally trained Bomb Disposal Technician in the military, and a close friend of Otis. Andrew's hiking business had been losing traction for quite some time. His soldier-like formality was still intact, standing tall despite the fall of his flailing business, which was evident through alarming financial reports showing consistent and increasing negative balance in his accounts.

"Right this way, detective." Andrew offered, leading him through the dense woods with the authority and precision that only a man with his specialized training would possess. Andrew diligently used his army skills to ensure the safety of hikers from any potential environmental dangers on their guided tours.

"Andrew-" Winston began, striding to keep up with the trained speedwalker, "I was told you two were close. And you had asked Otis about his insurance policy recently. Care to shed some light on that?"

Andrew did not look back as he continued walking. "Sure did. Otis had been open about his routine. I always knew when he was at the rink or off somewhere else. As for his insurance, he had approached me for advice and later updated it, naming me the beneficiary."

As they neared Andrew's hiking spot, Winston noticed a military-grade tent with tools, knives, ropes, canned food supplies, and hidden among them, explosives. Andrew's intense secrecy hinted at something more - these were not just regular hiking supplies.

"Quite a collection here, Andrew. Comes in handy during your hikes I presume?" Winston asked casually. Andrew replied with a nod, "It's an efficient system. Every item serves a purpose."

Before Winston could probe further, his phone buzzed, indicating a call from the station. "Just bear with me, Andrew," Winston excused himself. Andrew shuffled uncomfortably nearby, sparked a further conversation about Otis' recent insurance update.

A forensic update from the station linked the lethal grenade to the recent military base theft!

In the isolated serenity of a mountain cabin, tragedy strikes when Russell is discovered lifelessly slain, a shovel being the weapon of choice, prompting the seasoned Detective Winston to investigate the surrounding suspects, Naomi and Lloyd.

Seated in an office nestled midways between the city and the nearby mountains, Winston paced, waiting for his next interviewee. Lloyd, a local musician, and past resident of the rehab centers spread across the state, had been called in for questioning about the murder of Russell.

After a couple of moments, the door creaked open and in stepped Lloyd, his eyes darting round the dull police office. His lips were tightly closed, not to emit any nervous chuckles that might belittle his present state.

"You're Lloyd?" Winston asked, giving the man a scrutinizing look as he sipped his bitter coffee. "Yes, sir..." Lloyd replied, his voice barely above a whisper. Winston sighed and motioned for him to sit down.

From Winston's vantage, there was nothing extraordinary about him. Lloyd distinctly bore an air of normalcy, with nothing damning about him--except, perhaps, the recent discovery of a shovel in the car he'd apparently been spotted outside a local hardware store with. His friends had vouched for him, saying that carrying a shovel made sense given his past in landscaping, but those could easily be false confirmations. "What's a musician doing with a shovel in his car?" Winston mused aloud.

"Oh, that.." Lloyd shifted, seeming almost proud. "That comes from my past, you see. Been involved in many a landscaping project. Old habits hardly die, I guess."

Winston nodded, his eyes not leaving Lloyd as he mentioned Russell. "Apparently, you were with Russell up at that mountainside cabin, weren't ya?" Lloyd swallowed audibly, then nodded.

"I... I was." Lloyd confirmed. "He invited me for a weekend. I accepted and stayed there, sir."

"And do you happen to remember if there was anyone else there?" Winston's question pierced the room.

"No, sir. Just Russell and me. No one else." Lloyd's voice shook slightly, drenched in anxiety.

Winston shifted the focus of the conversation, his eyes zeroing on a batch of letters. "Russell was threatening to disclose these letters, wasn't he? He would expose your drug addiction to the band if you didn't step down," he probed, shuffling the documents as Lloyd's face turned pale.

"I couldn't let him tell the band... I fought so hard to keep that past behind," Lloyd murmured. "Those letters... they held my life's biggest regrets."

With that, Lloyd's confession was done. Winston felt a curious sense of unease existing in the otherwise silent room featuring the exhausted and quite possibly vulnerable Lloyd. Silently, his eyes followed Lloyd out of his office and felt the chill of the mountain cabin travel all the way down to his city office.

Winston cranked the heater in his car as he parked in front of the police station. He couldn't shake off the cold chill of the mountain crime scene. Russell, another good man gone too soon.

Reminiscing over evidence photos, he couldn’t help but eye the shovel. There it was, the suspected murder weapon itself. Unforeseen, such an everyday tool, now stained with malice.

Pulling up security camera footage on his laptop, he saw Naomi, Russell’s mother, digging in her garden. The timestamp indicated it was just the day before Russell’s murder. Winston made a mental note; Naomi had started a new gardening project at her home recently. The last thing Russell saw might have been rather ironic for him - the very shovel he used to help dig holes for his mother's flowers. 

The next morning after grabbing a coffee to go, Winston pulled up to Naomi’s house. 

“Detective Winston, how are you?” Naomi asked letting him inside.

“Morning, Ma’am. I’m here about Russell.” He replied, trying meticulously hard not to let his empathy show in his voice. 

“Yes, I thought as much,” She responded and motioned an invitation to sit down.

⟦Over⟧ coffee, Winston learned about Naomi's recent solitary hobbies. She told him about spending afternoons in the local park. Her neighbor had reported her midnight walks to the police. And her recent shunning of social events. Odd behavior, he debated, for a woman who just lost her son. Also noted her hands hardened and calloused from vigorous gardening work, reminded him of the footage.

“Russell came by the cabin last weekend. I had inherited it from my parents and was there alone all weekend. I had invited him over…” Her voice dropped, “And then I found him. Evidently when I was gardening...”

Her words hung in the air. Winston finished his coffee and excused himself. Time to go meet with her neighbor, perhaps they noticed something Naomi missed.<turn|>

In the eerie glow of a laser tag arena, Nelson's life tragically ended with an axe, leaving Detective Winston to navigate a web of deception spun by suspects Mackenzie and Erika.

Winston had barely blinked since he started pouring over the case files. Nelson, the financial auditor, was found murdered at a laser tag arena of all places, and the murder weapon: an axe. This was far from the norm and even stranger was the timing of the murder, coinciding with a laser tag game Nelson had been participating in.

The local PD had brought in Mackenzie for questioning. Winston noted she wore an expensive watch, as did Nelson. Seems they had more in common than he had first thought.

Winston entered the interrogation room. Mackenzie didn't look up. He started off the conversation as casually as possible.

"Heard you and Nelson went to play laser tag that very day," Winston asked, with a neutral expression.

"Yeah," answered Mackenzie, "He wanted to blow off some steam after working all day."

"Work must've been tough. Big pressure in the audit department," said Winston, maintaining his tone.

"A lot of discrepancies for sure," Mackenzie replied, her voice a tad more serious this time.

Interesting. Winston remembered Nelson had filed a complaint about anomalies with the funds in the company. He had to change the course of the enquiry slightly.

"I've heard they have some pretty secluded areas in these laser tag arenas. You were spotted heading into one of them shortly before the game during which Nelson was murdered, Mackenzie," said Winston, watching her face closely. She took a deep breath before speaking again.

"I used to work as a lumberjack. I got used to the quiet, you know?" she responded, her eyes never leaving his. "Used to throw axes in college as part of a sport, so I also went into those areas to relax when I had time between games."

Taking a pause himself, Winston said, "And this axe you've recently been seen with?"

"I took it with me that day," she admitted without hesitation. "Thought some kids might like to see some tricks. Used to show 'em off back in my lumberjack days."

Winston nodded, "You certainly know how to handle one."

Suddenly, Winston's phone buzzed with a message. He skimmed through the contents and glanced up at Mackenzie again, now studying her expensive accessories.

"Mackenzie, you made several large cash deposits recently," Winston said, still casual, "Uncommon for your pay grade, no?"

A flash of a defensive posture wasn't lost on Winston. But the room remained silent except for his ensuing words.

"Well, we can get to that later," Winston said standing up and walking to the door, "Take care, Mackenzie."

She nodded, her eyes now transfixed at the solitary light bulb above her.

After leaving the room, Winston exhaled a deep breath. He felt a strange energy from Mackenzie...an air of danger and desperation. But he had to stick to the facts, and the facts alone. Destiny, it seemed, had led him down an unusual path indeed.

Winston studied the crime scene report from the laser tag arena. Nelson was the victim this time. His eyebrows narrowed as he looked at the weapon of question - an axe. Quite a strange telling for such a place.

The next part of Winston’s day led him to Erika, Nelson's travel companion and a former lumberjack champion by trade. Erika was neither surprised by the detective or the fact he wanted to discuss Nelson's demise.

"Erika and Nelson entered the arena together and you were with him the entire time...," he asked in a questioning manner.

"Yes detective, Nelson and I both arrived together and I never left his side until...," she replied in a collected voice.

"An axe in a laser tag arena...," Winston sighed under his breath. Erika's ears seemed to pick on this and she acknowledged the odd presence of the tool.

"Yes, Detective... I noticed that toolbox. I even commented to Nelson about the axe inside it". Her lumberjack past echoed slightly in her voice as she spoke.

She didn't hide that she exhibited high axe-wielding skills - a fact that was common knowledge in her home town. She won numerous lumberjack competitions, after all.

During his investigation, Winston also found that Erika had a habit of using a VPN when browsing the internet, and that she cleared her browsing history after each session. He had to smile at this. In an age when everyone displayed their lives on social media, Erika's avoidance of the platform was quite unique. It was something Winston astutely noticed.

Confirming this observation was Gerald, a companion on their recent travel. "Erika, she's rather private when it comes to the internet. She stays away from social media, and I've seen her clear her browser history after each use," he noted in his conversation with Winston.

He found that confirmed by her college roommate as well. She blushed, then sheepishly said, "Yeah, Erika never really cared for social media. She's always been a private person."

"Erika, I find it quite peculiar that Nelson was found dead just minutes after you two entered the laser tag arena and were together," Winston finally expressed.

Erika's gaze shifted slightly at Winston’s last comment but she remained silent, her face a calm mask.<turn|>

In the cramped confines of an airplane mid-flight, Zoe was slain using a simple bottle of bleach, propelling Detective Winston into a sky-high murder mystery involving two main suspects: Russell and Alice.

Detective Winston traced his finger along the cleaning supply shelves on the upper deck of Russell's boat, eyeing the bleach conspicuously nestled between a bucket and a scrub brush. The boat bobbed upon the serene waves, while a plane passed overhead, reminding Winston of an earlier sighting.

He remembered seeing Russell boarding that particular plane; a coincidence which became crucial as the case developed.

"Russell," Winston began, involuntarily swaying a bit with the boat's movement, "You use these for cleaning the vessel?"

"Sure do. Learned that during my ship cleanup training. Bleach is requisite for keeping everything in shipshape," the sailor responded, stretching a calloused hand to pick up the vessel. "However, I had a bit of an accident with it once, spilled it on my hands causing harsh chemical burns. Not pleasant, I can tell you."

Russell's face hardened a bit as he set the bleach back in place, adding, somewhat awkwardly, "But what can you do? Matter of training, innit? We all follow procedures."

Winston nodded, making noncommittal noise in agreement. Then, he continued, "Russell, tell me about that trip... the one you took not long ago."

"Oh, that?" Russell scratched his head, "Nothing much to tell, I don't fly often, water is more my domain. But yeah, had to visit family, got a ticket for a coastal ride."

Winston leaned forward, observing Russell's expressions. "By coincidence, Zoe was also on that flight, wasn't she?" 

Russell stiffened slightly and Winston noticed the hint of worry crossing his eyes. "Yeah, small world, innit? She was there, sat right beside me for the entirety of the trip."

Inquiring further Winston said, “Did she seem jittery to you, Russell? I Received word that she's been contacting the police for quite some time, reporting offenses she's witnessed.”

Russell responded nervously, "Yeah, heard something similar...It made me uncomfortable, seeing how she started discussing her crime witnessings and all... Well, she even talked about some smuggler group... and I involuntarily disclosed my involvement in questionable activities. Honestly, it felt as if she had seen right through me.”

Winston noticed the worry in Russell's eyes again. He deduced it resulted from Zoe witnessing his wrongdoings and now disclosing these events to others, especially the police. Feeling the tension growing, Winston quickly shifted subjects, “There was even a time when she accepted a drink from you during the flight, didn’t she?”

Russell looked at him, just a hint of surprise in his eyes as he affirmed, "Yes. Yes, she did."

After leaving Russell, Winston couldn't help but think of Zoe and the courage she had exhibited. Zoe had revealed to a close friend about Russell's suspicious actions that looked a lot like drug smuggling. As Winston walked away, he marveled at this young woman's knack for uncovering truths and wondered who’d believe that her penchant for justice would lead her down this turbulent path.

Winston stood at the back of the airplane cabin, dull fluorescent lights casting an artificial pallor over the surrounding faces. There, in an almost eerie calm, sat Alice, the spiritual guru making her way to a retreat with Zoe. Alice was once a flight attendant and used to her guide her companions while flying, as can be seen by the way she carefully selected seats together while booking tickets for herself and Zoe for this flight. 

"Alice," Winston began, taking the empty seat next to the spiritual guru. She turned to him, her face flushed and lined with sweat. He noted a fidgety disposition coupled with nervous scratching and almost indecipherable mumbling, but he continued. "I heard you and Zoe were traveling together for a spiritual retreat. And, I remember a gossip at the airport that you specifically saw to it that your seats were together?"

Alice nodded, her hands shaking slightly. "Yes, that's why we bought the tickets together. I always get nervous during flights. Being seated close to my companion helps." 

Winston took that in, feeling a certain satisfaction at the beads of sweat dotting Alice's forehead. "And you were helping Zoe adjust with air travel like in your flight attendant days, right?"

"No," Alice said rapidly, her hands touched her chest, and then flittering over the bottles laying around her. "I... I just comfort her with my spiritual methods."

The detective's keen eyes took note of the bottles, their familiarity stinging his brain. Essential oil, but what interested Winston was the similarity they shared in shape and size with another bottle, a bleach bottle he remembered Alice once accidentally swallowed from in her past- the incident which maybe even led her towards understanding the spiritual practices involving bleach ingestion. 

"You've got quite the collection of bottles here, Alice."

She nodded hesitatingly, "For my spiritual practices. I was even researching the effects of bleach for cleansing... even after that incident where I accidentally swallowed a sip and had to go to the hospital. It got me interested, you see."

Winston let her words trail off, but his mind was racing. He looked at Zoe's empty seat, her preferred Dragonfruit punch still untouched. The same beverage, Winston noticed, that was in Alice's bag, suspiciously close to the bleach-shaped bottles. 

Before Winston got up to leave, he asked casually, "Was it you who had an exchange with an infamous drug dealer some time back? I believe I saw you handing over some money."

Alice's face⟦ turned⟧ whiter, if possible. "That man... he had a history of selling illegal drugs... but I was only buying... I..."

Winston left her there, mumbling to herself. He had his facts. The mystery wasn't solved, but the clues were there, and Winston turned away as he received a message on his phone. He wondered if the truth went even deeper than it seemed.<turn|>

In the seemingly peaceful city zoo, Stuart's life was brutally ended with a hatchet, and now it's up to Detective Winston to uncover the truth among suspects Xanthe and Lowell.

As Winston left the precinct, his mind was in a swirlwind. Investigating the murder of Stuart gave him a bone-chilling sensation. The images of the crime scene fresh in his mind. But a crime scene found in a zoo? He needed answers.

Entering the coffee shop where Xanthe worked as a barista, Winston could see several customers waiting in line. Apparently, their coffee was popular in town. Xanthe could be seen behind the bar, engaging her clients, before she gracefully hurried over to the espresso machine. In that hurry, she accidentally drops a piece of paper. A customer quickly pointed it out, and Winston intervened to pick it up. 

"That looks like a list of phone numbers," the customer said, peering over Winston's shoulder and noticing the peculiar numbers. "Those aren't usual business or personal contacts. I work in telecommunications, I know."

"Thank you," Xanthe said, acknowledging the mishap, before busying herself again. 

Winston headed to the bar but opted not to order anything. Instead, he scanned the fallen paper. The now identified phone numbers seemed quite out of place.  

The Zoo's visitor logs showed that Stuart was a regular, showing up daily. He made a mental note of that. There was certainly a connection between Stuart and the coffee shop...with the baristas. Stuart was seen being quite friendly with the baristas, including the newcomer, Mary, whom he praised quite often. 

"Was Stuart a regular here?" Winston asked Xanthe.

"Yes," She responded warmly, "he loved our coffee. Always praised Mary's hand.. She's pretty good, new or not. But you know, I was the one who used to make his coffee. Had his special recipe down, I did," She added, pointing towards a different espresso machine designated for complicated orders.

"Oh, that's interesting. You must have a busy schedule," Winston said offhandedly.

"Oh yeah, it includes working weekends too," Xanthe said, giving off a slight chuckle.

As Winston left the coffee shop, he recalled that Stuart's murder happened on a weekend. Winston knew this wasn't a coincidence, there was a complex web of intrigue developing here, leading him deeper into the mystery.

Winston stared at the emails on Stuart's computer screen, reading about the deep financial holes Lowell had dug for his bank’s high profile clients. The source of these emails was unidentified, but they were enough to start a full-scale fraud investigation. It appeared that the businessman had been trading emails with Stuart not too long ago. It wasn't too hard to figure out why Stuart might've been targeted.

He looked over the police report, his cigar glowing in the dim room. It was late afternoon when the banking industry slows its hustle and bustle, that Stuart was found at the zoo. The next stop for Winston would be the café. Sure enough, the receipts and CCTV footage confirmed that Lowell was a regular there as well and was there around the same time Stuart was at the zoo.

The guy at the lumber yard confirmed that Lowell came in pretty frequently, mostly for firewood and sometimes for tools. Strange, considering the murder weapon was a hatchet and it just so happened to match the brand that Lowell usually favored.

Winston noticed the respect she commanded. He also noticed the way her colleagues avoided looking at her—or rather, the tattoo inked to her arm. 

Before Winston could enquire further, a family passed by them. A group of kids laughing and shoving at each other, a remote jammed into the hands of Hailey as they settled onto a nearby couch.

"Movie night?" Winston asked and received an affirmative nod from her. "Yeah and nobody likes the movies I pick but it's my house so it's my rules."

Standing under the magnificent dome, Winston noticed Angela, Derek's grandmother who was a highly respected member of the community. She was absorbed in polishing a large silver key - clearly bestowed only to trusted insiders of the community. She appeared not to notice Winston's arrival.

As Winston made his presence known, Angela seemed startled but quickly masked her emotions. 

"My apologies for the intrusion, Ma’am. I am here about Derek," Winston delicately approached the subject.

Even though her face remained neutral, the flinch in her eyes revealed her disturbance. "That's quite alright, detective..." she started, her grip tight around the key.

"I remember Derek grinning over that photo; where he caught you secretly betting against him in the last competition," Winston probed. "He told me he intended to expose you at the upcoming one."

Angela's reaction suggested his words hit a nerve, "You see, Detective... Derek, he...knew something. He found proof of my betrayal. He confronted me about it, claimed he would tell everyone if I didn't stop it. I would lose everything."

As Winston prepared to leave, Angela asked, "Do you think this could have escalated beyond our fishing rivalry? Derek confronting me about the bets and all..."

"Autumn," I greeted her as I approached, "how are things?" 

She took a moment, reached down into her bag, and pulled out a specific thrilling novel titled "Perfect Crime". She glanced up from the book and responded, "Oh, hello Winston. Just the usual."

I looked down at her book, the title striking a chord, "This one any good?"

Autumn got excited and spoke in vivid detail about the perfect crime plotted in the novel. Her enthusiasm around the theme of crime and the specific details almost perturbed me, but I chose to focus on the dialogue at hand.

We mentioned Donald, and how he had plans⟦ to⟧ head to the bunker. Autumn froze for a moment before returning to her normal composure. "He trusted you," I said, "would have let you in the bunker."

"The bunker? Yeah, I know the place. Donald used to talk about it," she replied, trying to sound nonchalant. But I could discern a hint of unease in her voice, the knowledge of the bunker and everything that had transpired there appeared to weigh heavy on her.

Autumn had been in a gang with Donald. Back in the day, they used to own this town, running around and kicking up dust wherever they went. Time moved on, things had changed, but the past lingered in Autumn's fear of her past crimes revealing themselves.

Donald had confided in me once that he discovered Autumn was still engaging in criminal activities. She had psychic abilities which made her an asset in their criminal past and perhaps, in her current endeavours.

The clang of the door brought me back to the café. Autumn had left, the sunshine reflected off her hair as she headed down the street, her murder mystery novel tucked securely under her arm. The people in the café moved again, life resumed while questions circled in my mind. Along with Autumn, I left the café: one looking to uphold justice, and the other, potentially, to evade it.

"You've done some snake handling, haven't you?" - Winston asked.

Jay chuckled. "A rite of passage, they call it. Over there in the region with a high snake population, it’s a trial, a blessing, an exorcism.” His tone held a grim, respectful distance. 

Winston nodded, "I've heard it's common among missionaries to learn about snakebite remedies as well."

"A living antidote, in case of a bite, that's not common knowledge."- Jay answered, leaning back in his chair.

"Were you aware, Jay," Winston began, "that Donald discovered certain… irregularities?"

Jay's eyes flickered to Winston's for the first time. "Irregularities? You mean the smuggling?" He admitted.

Winston let the confession hang in the air between them.

"I was using the missions to distribute certain substances, that part is true." Jay said.

"You got trained here, in the bunker. Now you distribute substances, in religious ruse. " His tone turned pointedly menacing. 

He leaned in slightly, resting his elbows on the tabletop, "Discovery of which, Jay, would do a lot more than tarnish a reputation."

Jay remained silent, his eyes hardening and body rigid, awaiting the impending threat the detective presented. 

Winston suddenly backed off, taking his notes and exiting the room, leaving Jay alone among his thoughts.<turn|>

In the quiet solitude of a local library, Philip is found shockingly murdered with a barbed wire, leaving Detective Winston with the arduous task of sifting truth from alibis of the two main suspects, Hugo and Maria.

Winston's mind was buzzing during the ride to the local hair salon, a tragic incident sinking his spirits. Philip, a library frequenter, was dead, with dire circumstances suggesting a gruesome murder. The weapon, a coil of barbed wire, unusual for sure. As he walked into the salon, he saw a middle-aged woman, Maria with a multitude of barbed hairpins reflecting ominously under the lights. She was working away with a pair of scissors, her nimble fingers managing both the razor and the various hairpins with the dexterity of an artist.

"Maria?" Winston asked.

Caught off guard, Maria looked up, her eyes wide in surprise. "Yes, detective, can I help you with something?" she answered, never pausing her delicate dance of grooming. She clicked her scissors, moved on to her razor, then her infamous collection of barbed hairpins, all with the practiced ease of someone in her profession for a long time. 

"I hear you've been doing this for over fifteen years?" he asked, partially making small talk, partially feeling out the woman in front of him.

"Sixteen years, next Tuesday." She replied, her gaze deliberately focused on her current client's head. 

"Quite a long time..." Winston said, thoughtful. "You ever do hair for a fellow called Philip?"

Maria paused for a moment, her eyes downcast. "Yes, I did his hair once. He's the one found in the library, right?"

"Yes," Winston nodded, "I heard about your usual evening strolls to the library. The one open late till 10 pm?"

"Yeah, it's quiet, peaceful. They don't mind if I bring my coffee inside. I even have a key, just in case I lose track of time and it's closing," Maria disclosed.

"I see. How about Robert? Phillip's fiance. He been here, recently?" Winston changed the subject.

Maria swallowed and cleared her throat, stepping away from her customer to face Winston. "Yes, he came... to talk." 

"To talk about the wedding, or about that time in high school where you confessed your love to him before he proposed to Philip?" Winston probed.

Maria averted her eyes, "About the wedding... but, yes, we also brought up the past. I've been in love with Robert since high school, and I've been secretly carrying that love for years, you know."

Winston observed Maria. Things certainly aren't always as they seem, he thought, as she returned to her client, her barbed hairpins dancing in the slightly unsettling light. The fact that the time of Philip's death aligned eerily with Maria's usual library visit was an added layer of unease. "Well, Robert's supposed to marry Philip soon, isn't he?" 

"Yes, but things aren't always as they seem, detective." Maria's voice held an edge as she responded, her gaze being both hurt yet defiant, hinting at a deeper tale yet to unravel.

Blowing off steam, jumping from coffee shop to coffee shop, Winston was back on track, unanswered questions regarding Philip's mysterious murder bouncing in his mind. Known for his capacity for violence to get what he wanted, Philip had a reputation; ironically, barbed wire, his common form of conflict resolution, had been the weapon.

The detectives at the precinct were all a twitter about the eccentric sound technician, Hugo. Out of all potential suspects they'd drawn in, one thing about Hugo was blinking on Winston's radar. Not once had any colleague, friend or customer ever been invited to his personal studio where Hugo spent most of his time. The man was protective of his private space, it seemed. 

"I'm detouring to Hugo's office," Winston informed his partner as he made a left turn.

The professional layout of Hugo's studio stood testament to his skills. Winston noticed the different⟦ categories⟧ of wires neatly stowed away, labeled by type. Spools of common wires were neatly packed, then his gaze floated towards an unusual collection of unique wires, barbed wire included, labeled 'personal collection'. He stroked one with his gloved fingers, lost in thought.

"Hugo," Winston called for his attention, "This is some impressive collection. Not everyone works with barbed wire in a sound system, huh?" Hugo's smile was gentle, "I just like to keep my wire knowledge versatile," he shrugged.

"I heard you missed out on this year's industry conference," Winston inquired casually. 

"Yeah. Conferences are not my cup of tea," Hugo chuckled, "Too much show and too little know. I prefer focusing on the actual job, here in my studio."

Casual chat moved reflective as Winston asked about Philip, "What about Philip? Ever get into a formal tussle with him?" Hugo's rifle through a box of cables paused, "No direct confrontation, sir, but I was an unfortunate audience to threats he made to my brother over a phone call. Nastiest conversation ever."

Winston nodded, taking in the distraught sound engineer before himself. Hugo's brother owed a significant amount to Philip, everyone and their nephew knew that. It had been no blind gamble, but rather a bet gone awry. It had complicated Hugo's personal dynamics, certainly. Especially so since no one saw Hugo at the annual company holiday party. Usually a regular, Hugo's absence sent alerts.

Duty kept Hugo traveling between different venues for sound gigs, with a vast array of tools tagging all along, wires included, also, wires very similar to the ones found at Philip's crime scene. Winston mulled over this kaleidoscope of details, knowing well the devil lay in their details, as he drove back to the precinct.<turn|>

In the dim light of his office, detective Winston thumbed through the flight records of one Hector Barbosa, a flight attendant for an international airline. His recent travel logs had him shuttling multiple times to and from South America, the only place where the frog that produces a toxic poison can be found. In just a few weeks of travels, he managed to visit the region several times. Closing the file, Winston grabbed his coat and made his way to Hector’s residence.

Upon arrival at Hector's home, Winston was greeted with an impressive gallery of artwork. Though it seemed grim and somewhat macabre, a theme Hector had expressed enthusiasm for in conversation, Winston had to admit, Hector had talent. Each painting was meticulously detailed and chillingly realistic, with gruesome scenes of death and despair. Hector escorted him through, speaking of his passion and backgrounds; studying biology, specializing in amphibians, particular those native to South America, before taking a recent turn into the fast-paced life as a flight attendant.

Winston moved through the house, noting the unusual abundance of crimson. 

“New project?” He asked. 

“A passion piece...” Hector responded, pointing out to a fresh canvas that sat in the corner, a pot of fresh crimson red paint on an easel next to it that Winston instantly recognized. He'd seen Hector carrying it home from the art supply store earlier.

The following morning Winston placed another visit, this time to the local skate park. Public records indicated both Hector and Roxanne, the⟦ victim⟧, frequent activity in this park, perhaps an emblem of their youth, or simply an outlet to unwind. Even here, halfway across the world, Hector was diligent about signing in, a habit that placed him in the vicinity of the crime scene during the murder.

"Hector Barbosa" was clearly listed on the sign-in sheet on the day of the murder. The times matched the timeframe of Roxanne's murder as recorded by the coroner. With no convincing alibi during the time, this only intensified the the suspicion on Hector. 

Winston shoved the paperwork back in his satchel as he stood up to leave. It was time to head back to the office. After taking a last look at the desolate skate park, Winston set a course back to his office. He had a long night of sifting through evidence and connecting the dots ahead of him.

Detective Winston rubbed his temples, going over the case again. It had started with Roxanne, found dead in a skate park one hectic morning. The cause of death had been unusual...poison from a frog. Now his attention was on Stacey, having been seen at the skate park the same day of the murder.

"I did see her there that day...she always came to the same spot, worked on her designs..." the teenage skater he was interviewing stomped his skate on a piece of wood. "Used to be pro, you know, forefront of the game... Then when Roxanne got big, doing all the flashy moves...people started calling her out..."

It was true, Winston reflected as he thanked the skater for his time, Stacey was known in combative sports as an expert. But her athleticism isn't the reason why she fell into his radar. The local pet store owner had a strange tale.

"Yup, she came in the other day and bought a peculiar pet, one of those exotic poison dart frogs... expensive, bright colors..." The pet shop owner, a tattooed man in his fifties, explained. Winston recalled his previous conversation with Stacey. She had openly talked about her trips to rainforests, being an avid hiker, often running into wildlife. She had even mentioned her interest in studying about poison dart frogs.

The day had grown long. Winston returned to the skate park, standing where Stacey would habitually be. Having talked to a number of witnesses who confirmed Stacey’s presence during the same time Roxanne would be...too coincidental he mused. 

"Roxanne liked this spot too...it became her spot after she started ripping off Stacey's designs. Strange, isn't it?" a skateboarder mulled, watching him curiously, "To die in a place where you've stolen so much?"

With Roxanne's sudden rise to stardom, a career that fed off Stacey's unique designs, he had a sense he was close... if only he could outpaint the whole picture.  

"Roxanne didn't care," a girl clad in ripped jeans and a baggy sweatshirt frowned, the anger seeping through her defiant tone, "Even when Stacey begged her to stop, she didn't care...said she'd made them better."

In the deafening silence of an unexpectedly deserted fitness center, Detective Winston finds himself staring at a chilling scene - Isaac's lifeless body riddled with shotgun pellets, leaving Milton and Alice as his primary suspects.

It was one of those sweltering afternoons, the humidity thick and relentless, as Detective Winston walked into the buzzing energy of the local fitness center. Remnants of police tape lingered in corners, while somber-touches reminders of what had happened to Isaac still hung in the air.

He was here to interview Milton, a well-known landlord in the vicinity and interestingly enough, an aficionado of funeral practices. As a testament to the latter, he often locked himself away to watch documentaries about funeral practices, a behavior reported by several tenants. Milton's fascination was no secret.

Winston stepped into Milton's office, spotting a wall lined with framed contents. Among them was a gun license, recently issued by the local authorities - a fitting addition, given that Milton had passed all mandatory firearms training courses.

Oddly enough, Milton was seated behind his desk clad in a sharp, well-cut black suit. This wasn't out of character though; this was a man known for appearing overdressed for simple occasions. In fact, a tenant had once mentioned that Milton regularly shops for coats and ties at funeral shops.

Winston spotted a shotgun in a corner, a disturbing sight considering it was the same type specified in the coroner's report for Isaac's death. It was an intriguing piece of evidence, considering Milton owns the shotgun.

Their conversation veered into various topics, with Milton highlighting his passion for reading. His bookshelf was lined with an extensive collection of books on death rituals from around the world - yet another proof of his peculiar interests. 

In the midst of their conversation, Isaac's name came up. Following reliable sources, Winston knew something crucial - Isaac had stumbled upon evidence directly implicating Milton in a tax evasion scheme. Isaac, the ever-vigilant whistleblower, was preparing to expose Milton's scandalous scheme - a revelation that could land Milton in prison.

As Winston left the fitness center, he pondered on his findings. Milton's tax evasion scheme, his interest in funeral practices, the shotgun license, the matching murder weapon... it all seemed to connect. He was confident that the tax evasion evidence would be enough to send Milton to jail, but for now, only time would tell. It was just another day on the job for Winston. As for Milton, his fate hung in the balance.

Detective Winston studied the scene: shattered glass, blood splatter, and scattered workout equipment telling a silent story. The fitness center wasn't the usual type of crime scene he found himself in. He sighed deeply and headed over to his prime suspect: Alice.

Alice was just a stone's throw away from the crime scene. Staring blankly with pale, emotionless eyes. In her hand, a shotgun; paperwork indicating a fresh purchase tucked within its case, valid purchase documents all checked out at the base.

Winston approached Alice cautiously and asked, "You know Isaac's workout routine, correct? The list of Isaac's routines you've given us earlier... it matches the information we gathered. You both were here all the time." 

Shocked by the sudden personal query, Alice confessed, "We workout together, Winston. At least... we used to."

Winston's eyes flickered to the shotgun slackly rested in Alice's lap. "Been a while since I've seen a lady with a new piece like this."

Alice was quick to correct him, "Not to boast, Winston, but I've been handling such arms ever since my military days."

Despite the grim predicament, Winston could tell Alice was trying to be cooperative. She was calm, composed; despite the whole flare-up. He moved on to the next line of questioning, "Your son... he interacted often with Isaac?"

Alice appeared apprehensive before finally admitting, "Recently, yes... He told me Isaac threatened him. Isaac... he acted aggressively towards my boy often."

"Interesting," Winston stammered, not wanting to press Alice too hard. He asked a softer question to lighten the mood, "You often workout together then?"

Alice looked surprised and retorted mockingly, "Is it that weird? We were the members of the same fitness center after all."

Before Winston could continue his questioning, he was handed a document by one of his officers. It read Isaac’s name and the note of a restraining order filed against him by a previous ex-partner. It seemed complicating factors always came in multiples in cases such as this.

Without keeping Alice in the dark, he disclosed the information with her, “A restraining order, and a school expulsion due to fighting incidents... Isaac seemed to have some rough patches in the past, huh?”

Alice turned her head and acknowledged Winston's statement with a slight nod, her lips sealed shut.

Winston wasn't sure why, but he felt the need to reassure her and said, "We're in this together, Alice. We'll figure it out. If Isaac was threatening your son, then we can't overlook any facet of the situation."

Seeing Alice with a newly purchased shotgun in her possession and catching onto bits of their relationship, Winston tried to figure out the puzzle, leaving no stone unturned. The interview with Alice wasn't offering any easy solutions, but Winston knew the case was anything but such.<turn|>

Winston adjusted the brim of his hat as he stepped through the automatic door, the smell of fresh flowers overwhelming his senses. He immediately took notice of the intense atmosphere, the air heavy, the shop's occupants quiet. Looking around, he saw Ruben, the owner of the florist's shop, immersed in his work—grinding powder in a mortar, measuring volatile liquids with a dropper, and then mixing it all.

"Busy I see," Winston remarked. 

Ruben glanced up, his bright green eyes flicking towards a book on the counter. Winston caught sight of the cover, reading 'Veterinary Medicine: An Essential Guide.' Ruben’s passion for learning was no new news. When he wasn't caught up in his flower shop, he was often seen engrossed in text about animal physiology, relating it to his plant biology knowledge.

"Just preparing the floral preservative mix for tomorrow," Ruben said, pointing towards the array of acids lined in front of him. "Acetic acid, my boy, along with citric and ascorbic acids - they all work wonders for a bouquet."

"You studied Chemistry, I've heard," Winston remarked casually.

Ruben smiled at this. "You need a sense for it in my line of work - keep the flowers fresh and so on. He peered at the detective over vintage spectacles, "We're a lot like the plants you know, animals. From the way we grow to the way we die. There's beauty in knowing the biology of it all."

Winston nodded, trying not to seem too interested. He noticed a customer coming out of the shop, a red rose in one hand with a distinct feather stuck to its stem - a feather lifelike, seemingly belonging to a bird species widely used in taxidermy.

Ruben's eyes lit up. "A bird feather, eh? Quite interesting.”

Winston didn't respond, simply turned to scan the shop, his eyes falling on a young girl huddled in a corner, eyes red with recent tears. That, he knew, was Ruben's niece. Word had reached him about the threats she'd received from a certain Henry, along with reports of Henry's inappropriate behavior toward her. It appeared to have escalated lately, visibly taking a toll on the poor girl.

Ruben noticed Winston’s gaze. “That’s my niece. She’s had a tough time of late." His words were somber, "We've had to handle some... unpleasantness. Threats from Henry, not to mention his behavior toward her..."

"Inappropriate behavior?" Winston asked, seeking confirmation.

Ruben nodded before sighing deeply. "Yes. That man had been threatening her, you know. His words, his actions... all wrong. Someone had to stand up for her..."

"I understand," Winston said. He picked up his hat and headed toward the door. As he turned around for one last look, he could see Ruben cleaning some glassware. A variety of corrosive chemicals, all meticulously labeled and aligned, surrounded him.

Winston leaned back in the shabby chair, hands folded, and stared unblinkingly across the table. Under the dismal light sat Michael, an archaeologist infamous for his carefree treatment of dangerous substances at the workspace. Michael was known for his reckless use of acid, a skill trained meticulously during his years at the archaeology institute studying the safe handling and disposing of dangerous substances. But he took this to a detrimental level, often taking home acid from work for his own personal use, much to people’s horror.

Michael was no stranger to trouble at work as well. He had been caught multiple times not only irresponsibly handling acid, but also indulging in drug use - specifically heroin. His frequent use often rendered him in states of significant intoxication.

"The vineyard incident, you were there Michael? Specifically in the secluded part where you had invited Henry to meet?" Winston asked.

Michael seemed surprised by the question but quickly regained composure. "Yes, I had invited Henry for a stroll around the secluded part of the vineyard. We crossed paths there quite regularly."

"Henry..." Winston whispered. Unfortunately, Henry wasn't just any other man for Michael. Henry's lifeless body was discovered soon after their encounter at the vineyard, right in the secluded area where Michael had invited him and where they were known to frequent.

"And you've used acid at work for artifact cleaning, right? Even took liberties to use it inappropriately?" Winston pried further.

"Yes," Michael replied curtly, with an ironic smile clinging to his face, “Taking it for a stroll from work to home wasn’t the best idea.”

Winston grunted, his gaze shifting to the visible injection marks on the man's arms. “You’ve been caught using heroin, haven’t you, Michael?”

Michael, almost seeming to read Winston’s thought, confessed, "Yes, heroin is my problem. Been caught for it more times than I can count."

"But it wasn't only your problem, was it, Michael? Henry... he knew and threatened to expose you,” Winston stated matter-of-factly.

Michael's confidence waivered. He stuttered, “Yeah... He did. He was going to tell everyone.”

"On records, you have intense training in handling acid and other substances,” Winston pointed out, “At the vineyard too, nobody saw you leave from the secluded part."

Michael fell silent. Fear was visible in his eyes. His hands clenched tightly into fists.
